newsitem.title: UK: EMI plans welcomed but stirs some criticism.
newsitem.headline: EMI plans welcomed but stirs some criticism.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute, the forerunner of the European Central Bank, on Friday unveiled its proposals for the mechanisms that will ensure Europe has a strong, credible monetary policy from 1999.

In a report published in Frankfurt, the EMI unveiled a set of monetary policy instruments for the future central bank, but made clear the final decisions on several key outstanding issues would have to be made by the ECB itself.
Britain cautiously welcomed the report but said it would fight to ensure it was not disadvantaged if it chose not to join a single currency.
The new central bank will not be up and running until next year and will assume monetary policy responsibility for Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) from the start of 1999.
The report shows the new bank will use monetary policy instruments very close to those of the German Bundesbank.

It will offer funds to banks at two main rates which will set the floor and ceiling for money market rates, similar to the role performed by the Bundesbank's Lombard and discount rates. Open market operations will be its main policy tool.
The report recommended the bank target either inflation or money supply but had eliminated the possibility of exchange rate targeting, interest rate pegging or nominal income targeting.
It said these three strategies did not fit in with the general principles it had set for the ECB's strategy.

It left open the question of whether the bank would use minimum reserves -- which require banks to deposit some funds at the central bank -- in its policy. The Bundesbank has pushed hard for the inclusion of this instrument.
Many European bankers were quick to criticise the idea of a reserve requirement, which some said would amount to a tax on the sector.
But EMI President Alexandre Lamfalussy said gradual changes in the use of the minimum reserve requirement in recent years had considerably reduced the burden imposed on banks.

"If I observe the last five to 10 years what I have been seeing is the evolution of reserve requirement techniques which has considerably diminished this tax, this burden on the banks," Lamfalussy told a news conference.

The British Bankers Association (BBA), which represents more than 300 British and overseas banks active in Britain, said in a statement the imposition of reserve requirements was "unnecessary for the efficient conduct of monetary policy and threatened to distort the market".
Reserve requirements are the percentage of bank deposits that firms must set aside with their central bank. Lowering or raising this requirement effectively influences money supply.

BBA Director-General Tim Sweeney said such a move would also lead to business moving away from the area covered by the euro, while his Luxembourg counterpart Lucien Thiel said it may lead to a two-tier system.
The Federal Association of German Banks, which represents private sector banks in Germany where a reserve requirement is currrently in force, called the mechanism superfluous.
The French banking association suggested if that if reserve requirements were imposed, they should bear interest. The Bank of England also said it argued against reserve requirements.
The British central bank also voiced its comments on another area of disagreement. On access to a settlement system known as TARGET, it said there remained an unresolved debate.
British bankers said they would fight to ensure Britain was not disadvantaged by being denied access to a new cross-border bank settlement system if it remained outside the euro bloc.
But Germany is unhappy about allowing countries outside EMU full access to euro funds, fearing this will disrupt efforts to control European monetary policy.
The EMI report saidthe central banks of countries outside the single currency would not be able to extend overnight credit in the euro to institutions in their countries.
But the Bank of England says all EU nations should have equal access to intraday credit and does not see this as an obstacle to the smooth conduct of monetary policy.

Lamfalussy said the Euro would benefit from the rapid development of a Euro-denominated bond market which would become an alternative to investment in dollar paper, and could become a general reserve currency.
Its ability to rival the dollar would depend, at least in part, on how quickly capital markets issue and trade debt in the new unit, the EMI said.
Economists reckon a single currency launched even with only a handful of EU countries would result in the second largest bond market in the world after the United States.
The EMI noted that the Maastricht Treaty made absolutely clear that the ECB had to make price stability its top priority.
However some economists said technicalities alone would not help the ECB withstand potential political pressure for a weaker euro after 1999, especially if unemployment remains high.
